nameStory: Plains coreopsis gets its common name from its love of open grasslands and prairies across the Great Plains. The genus name 'Coreopsis' comes from Greek words meaning 'bug-like,' referring to the shape of the seeds, while 'tickseed' refers to how these small, dark seeds resemble tiny ticks.
description: Plains coreopsis is a cheerful annual wildflower that brightens fields and roadsides with its golden-yellow daisy-like blooms. This slender plant typically grows 1-4 feet tall with delicate, feathery foliage that gives it an airy appearance. Each flower head features bright yellow petals (usually 8) that often have dark reddish-brown centers, creating a classic 'bulls-eye' pattern. It's a hardy pioneer species that thrives in disturbed soils and open sunny areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers with 8 notched petals surrounding a dark reddish-brown center disc that feels slightly raised and bumpy to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thin, deeply divided leaves that feel delicate and feathery, arranged oppositely on the lower stem and alternately higher up

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, branching annual that grows 1-4 feet tall with a loose, open appearance and multiple flower heads

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, elongated seeds that are slightly curved and smooth to the touch, resembling tiny ticks

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, green to reddish stems that feel firm but not woody, branching extensively in the upper portions

habitat: In New England, plains coreopsis is typically found in disturbed areas like roadsides, old fields, and cultivated areas where the soil has been turned over. It prefers full sun and well-drained soils, often appearing in waste areas, vacant lots, and along railroad tracks. This adaptable wildflower thrives in poor soils where many other plants struggle.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring, producing small rosettes of feathery leaves close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Blooms prolifically from mid-summer through early fall, with peak flowering in July and August when the bright yellow flowers are most abundant.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering into early fall while producing and dispersing seeds, with plants beginning to turn brown and dry as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving behind dried stems and scattered seeds that will germinate the following spring.

funFact: Plains coreopsis is such a prolific seed producer that a single plant can generate over 2,000 seeds, and these seeds can remain viable in the soil for up to 7 years, waiting for the perfect conditions to sprout!
confusionNotes: Plains coreopsis is most easily confused with other yellow composite flowers like black-eyed Susan, but coreopsis has notched petal tips (like tiny bites taken out) while black-eyed Susan has smooth, unnotched petals. Memory trick: 'Coreopsis has cuts in its petals.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'plains' coreopsis, this adaptable wildflower has spread far beyond the Great Plains and is now found across most of North America. It's also commonly called 'calliopsis' in garden centers, which can confuse beginners looking for the same plant under different names.
compareHints: Plains coreopsis differs from other New England coreopsis species by being an annual (dies each year) rather than perennial, and by having the most deeply divided, feathery leaves of the group. Rose coreopsis has pink flowers and grows in wetlands, while lance-leaved coreopsis has simple, undivided leaves and larger flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rose Coreopsis is the only tickseed in New England with pink or white petals - all its relatives like Lance-leaved and Whorled Coreopsis have bright yellow flowers.
Among its tickseed relatives, Whorled Coreopsis is the only one with thread-like leaves arranged in distinct whorls around the stem.

Lance-leaved Coreopsis differs from other Coreopsis species by its simple, unlobed lance-shaped leaves - Rose Coreopsis has much smaller pink flowers, while Whorled Coreopsis has very finely divided, thread-like leaves.
Tall coreopsis dwarfs all other New England coreopsis species - most relatives like lance-leaved coreopsis and rose coreopsis stay under 3 feet tall.

Among New England's coreopsis species, lobed coreopsis is immediately distinguished by its uniquely shaped leaves - rose coreopsis has narrow linear leaves, lance-leaved has simple spear-shaped leaves, and whorled coreopsis has thread-like leaves in circles around the stem.

Large-flowered tickseed stands out from other New England tickseeds by its size - both the flowers and overall plant are notably larger than rose coreopsis (which has pink flowers) or lance-leaved coreopsis.

Unlike its New England relatives like Lance-leaved Coreopsis (which has simple, narrow leaves) or Rose Coreopsis (which has thin, needle-like leaves), Prairie Coreopsis has those distinctive deeply-divided, finger-like leaves that make it unmistakable.
